title: Auditing Sabotage Bench: A Benchmark for Detecting and Fixing Research Sabotage in ML Codebases
claim: An adversarial red-team/blue-team protocol: one party corrupts a trusted artifact, the other must detect which version it received and repair it.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right flow, honest and sabotaged tracks, color-coded team boxes
description: A single flow diagram with two parallel tracks. The top track sits in a green shaded region labeled 'Honest Paper and Codebase'. It runs from 'Research question and methodology' to 'Honest implementation' to a 'Results' bar chart (A higher than B, in green). The bottom track sits in an orange region labeled 'Sabotaged Paper and Codebase'. It runs from the same research question box to 'Sabotaged implementation' to an 'Incorrect Results' bar chart (B higher than A, in red). A red arrow runs from the honest implementation down to the sabotaged one. It passes a pink 'Red Team: Attacker' box that shows robot or human+robot icons. Both result boxes feed a yellow oval, 'Randomly pick one', which has a coin icon. A blue arrow runs from the oval to 'Sabotage % + Proposed Fixes'. A light-blue 'Blue Team: Auditor' box sits above that arrow. The eye goes first to the colored team boxes and the contrasting bar charts.
caption: Methodology. The red team modifies the codebase implementation to produce qualitatively different results without changing the high-level methodology. The blue team receives either the honest or sabotaged version and must determine which and propose fixes.
abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to conduct research autonomously, misaligned systems could introduce subtle flaws that produce misleading results while evading detection. We introduce Auditing Sabotage Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the ability of auditors to detect and fix sabotage in ML research codebases. Our benchmark consists of 9 ML research codebases with sabotaged variants that produce qualitatively different experimental results. Each sabotage modifies implementation details, such as hyperparameters, training data, or evaluation code, while preserving the high-level methodology described in the paper. We evaluated frontier LLMs and LLM-assisted human auditors on our benchmark and found that both struggled to reliably detect and fix sabotage: the best performance was an AUROC of 0.77 and a top-1 fix rate of 42%, achieved by Gemini 3.1 Pro. We also tested LLMs as red teamers and found that LLM-generated sabotages were weaker than human-generated ones but still sometimes evaded same-capability LLM auditors. We release the benchmark to support research on monitoring and auditing techniques for AI-conducted research.
